physical_harm: The deceased was assaulted with a weapon, resulting in fatal injuries.
number_of_offences: Four offences were charged, but only one was finally upheld.
key_evidence_accepted: The dying declaration Exh. 21 has a ring of truth. The deceased specifically deposed to the clothes worn by the assailant. PW-13, who witnessed the incident, corroborated the nature of the apparel worn by the accused. Clothes recovered from the appellant matched the description. Stains on the clothes matched the blood group of the deceased. Medical evidence is consistent with ocular evidence.
witness_credibility: PW-13, the beat constable, was on duty and his presence at the incident location was natural. His statement that he was assigned to duty at the place of the incident was not cast in doubt. The mere fact that panch witnesses turned hostile is no reason to discredit the prosecution's case.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 10 July 1988; Trial judgment: 10 July 1989; High Court decision: 18 March 2006; Supreme Court decision: 24 January 2019
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Sushil Karanjkar; Counsel for the State: Nishant Ramakantrao Katneshwarkar
investigation_status: FIR registered under Sections 326 and 307 read with Section 34 of the Penal Code; charge sheet filed; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Acquittal; High Court: Convicted under Section 304 Part II; Supreme Court: Dismissed the appeal, upheld High Court's conviction
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant was the assailant, citing the dying declaration of the deceased, the testimony of PW-13 (the beat constable), the blood-stained clothes recovered from the appellant, and the medical evidence consistent with the ocular evidence. They also emphasized that the High Court correctly reversed the trial court's acquittal due to a miscarriage of justice.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the trial court's acquittal was justified, citing discrepancies in the investigation, the lack of direct identification of the appellant by PW-13, the failure to conduct a test identification parade, the hostility of certain witnesses, and the absence of examination of key witnesses like Lt. Melvin Desouza and the accompanying beat constable.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that an appellate court is justified in reversing an order of acquittal if it suffers from perversity and results in a miscarriage of justice, as established in K Gopal Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh and Chandrappa v. State of Karnataka.
precedent_relied_upon: K Gopal Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1979) 1 SCC 355 : [1979] 2 SCR 265; Chandrappa v. State of Karnataka (2007) 4 SCC 415 : [2007] 2 SCR 630; Mookiah v. State, Rep. by Inspector of Police, Tamil Nadu (2013) 2 SCC 89 : [2013] 2 SCR 881; Murugesan v. State, through Inspector of Police (2012) 10 SCC 383 : [2012] 13 SCR 1; Prem Singh v. State of Haryana (2013) 14 SCC 88 : [2013] 10 SCR 51
sentencing_rationale: The High Court convicted the appellant under Section 304 Part II of the IPC and sentenced him to five years' rigorous imprisonment because the incident was preceded by a quarrel, and thus did not attract the provisions of Section 302. The High Court found the charge against the appellant established beyond reasonable doubt.
other_sentence_order: The appellant was ordered to surrender to undergo the sentence, and the bail bonds were cancelled.
